First-time salon visits can be nerve-wracking, especially for anyone who's had a bad experience before — a stylist who didn't understand their hair, a consultation that got rushed, a cut or color that didn't match what was asked for. I take new-client visits at Studio Salon seriously for exactly that reason. Here's what to expect, start to finish, so you walk in ready and walk out with hair you love.

## Booking: Call or Text for Now

Right now, the easiest way to book with me at Studio Salon is to call or text (510) 690-5274. Online booking is on the way — we're finishing the setup — but for new clients, a short phone or text conversation actually works better anyway. It lets me ask a few questions before we lock in a time: what service you're looking for, the current state of your hair, how much length we're working with, any color history, and whether you've worn the style before.

A knotless install and a single-process color, for example, need very different time blocks, and I'd rather build your appointment accurately than squeeze you in and rush the work. If you text, please include your name, the service you're interested in, and a couple of days that work for you. I'll text back within a business day with available windows and a deposit link if one is needed.

Don't worry about sounding formal. This is a salon, not a doctor's office. A short "Hey, I'm trying to book a retwist, here's what my hair looks like" is plenty to start the conversation.

## The Consultation: Short, Honest, No Pressure

Every first visit starts with a quick consultation in the chair before any hair gets touched. Depending on the service, this is anywhere from five to fifteen minutes. I'll ask about your hair history — past chemical processes, last haircut, how your hair usually behaves after washing — and I'll actually look at your scalp and ends.

If you're coming in for color, I'll do a strand test if there's any uncertainty. If you're coming in for locs, I'll walk you through what your starter method looks like, how long initial locking typically takes, and what to expect in the awkward months in between.

If what you asked for isn't going to work on your hair — and sometimes that's the honest answer — we'll talk through alternatives before we start, not after. I'd rather reschedule you for the right service than send you out with something you don't love. No pressure, no upsell, no guilt.

## What to Bring Based on Your Service

What you bring depends on what you booked. Here's a simple guide by service type.

### For loc appointments

Come with clean, fully dried hair unless we've agreed on a wash service that day. Bring any products you currently use on your locs so I can see what's on the hair and decide whether we need to clarify. If you've had work done elsewhere recently, a couple of photos of the previous retwist really help me see where we're starting.

### For braids and protective styles

Come with freshly washed, detangled, and blow-dried hair, or add a wash-and-blow service to your booking so we can do it together. Bring the synthetic or human hair for your install; I'll tell you exactly how many packs when we book. Bring reference photos on your phone — three or four is better than one, and screenshots of the back of the style are underrated.

### For color

Come with hair that hasn't been washed that morning. A little natural oil on the scalp actually protects it during processing. Bring photos of the color you want and, if you have them, photos of colors you don't want. If you've had any box color in the last year, tell me even if you think I won't notice.

## Getting to 2902 Sacramento St

Studio Salon is at 2902 Sacramento St in Berkeley, in the Sacramento Street corridor between Ashby and Russell. Street parking is free and usually available within a block or two, though it gets tighter in the late afternoon. If you have a longer appointment, I'd plan to arrive ten minutes early so parking doesn't stress you out.

If you're coming from further in the East Bay or from San Francisco, Ashby BART is about a fifteen-minute walk or a very short rideshare from the shop. Several AC Transit lines run along Sacramento Street too. If you're driving from Oakland, Emeryville, Richmond, or Albany, you're looking at fifteen to twenty-five minutes on a normal day, longer if you hit rush hour on the 580 or 80.

On arrival, look for the Studio Salon sign. If the door is locked — it sometimes is between appointments — text the salon line and I'll let you in. There's no big waiting room; this is an intimate studio, not a chain. Please don't arrive more than five to ten minutes early, so the client ahead of you gets their full time.

## What the Session Actually Looks Like

Once you're settled in the chair, we'll do a final walk-through of the service we agreed on and any adjustments that came out of the consultation. For locs, expect a relaxed pace — retwists run about ninety minutes to two hours depending on your head count and the method we're using. Starter locs and first-time installs run longer.

For braids, plan for a long session. Four to eight hours is normal for a full head of knotless, and longer for elaborate tribal feed-ins. I'll give you breaks, water, and a chance to stretch. Please eat before you come, and bring a snack for the middle if you know you get hungry.

For color, processing time happens with you comfortable in the chair, and I may run a quick second service during that window if scheduling allows. Color appointments generally run two to five hours.

Throughout, feel free to ask questions. I actually like when clients are curious — it's a sign you're going to take care of the hair between visits. Bring headphones, a laptop, a book, whatever makes you comfortable. This is your chair for the duration.

## Leaving the Chair: Aftercare Expectations

Before you leave, I'll walk you through aftercare for whatever we just did. For locs: when to wash, which products are fine, which to avoid, and when to come back for your next retwist. For braids: sleep on satin, mist your scalp, and how long this set should live before take-down. For color: don't wash for at least forty-eight hours, use color-safe products, and please don't swim in chlorine for the first week unless you've coated your hair in a heavy leave-in first.

You'll leave with my contact, so if anything feels off in the first few days you can text me. A little soreness on day one after braids is normal; pain, bumps, or sores are not, and I want to know about those fast so we can adjust.

Most clients book their next appointment before they leave, which helps me hold slots during busy seasons and helps you stay on a sustainable schedule.

## Ready to Book? Here's the Next Step

If you've read this far, you're probably close to booking, and I'd love to see you. Call or text me at (510) 690-5274 with your name, the service you want, and a couple of days that work for you. If you're not sure which service you need, just tell me that. I'll ask the right questions and help you land on something that actually fits your hair and your life.

Studio Salon is at 2902 Sacramento St, Berkeley, serving clients across the East Bay. Welcome to the chair.

content:
Protective styling is the backbone of most natural-hair routines, but "protective" doesn't mean the same thing across every technique. The difference between a knotless box braid, a feed-in cornrow, and a crochet install comes down to how the hair is added, how tension is distributed, and how long the style will live on your head. Here's what I walk clients through at Studio Salon before we book anything, so you can pick the style that actually fits your hair.

## What Makes a Style "Protective"

The phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let's define it. A protective style tucks your natural ends away, limits daily manipulation, and — ideally — lets your hair retain length and moisture over weeks instead of days. Braids, twists, crochet installs, wigs over cornrows, and faux locs all qualify when they're done and maintained well.

What disqualifies a style? Too much tension, synthetic hair that abrades your edges, or leaving it in so long that your own hair mats at the root. A good install should feel snug on day one, loosen up by day three, and come out in six to eight weeks with your own hair intact.

The three styles I get asked about most at Studio Salon — knotless, feed-in, and crochet — each sit in a different spot on the protective-style spectrum. Knotless is the gentlest at the root. Feed-in is the cleanest-looking from the front. Crochet is the fastest to install. Understanding the trade-offs helps you pick what actually fits your hair, your budget, and your schedule here in Berkeley and the East Bay.

## Knotless Braids, Explained

Knotless braids start with a tiny section of your natural hair and feed extensions in gradually as the braid progresses down the length. There's no knot at the root, which is the defining difference from traditional box braids. The look is flatter at the scalp, the tension is dramatically lower, and — most importantly for fine or fragile hair — there's no hard bump pulling on your roots for the entire life of the style.

Knotless works on nearly every texture, from looser curl patterns to tightly coiled 4C, and it's especially good for clients with tender scalps, edge damage, or a history of breakage at the hairline. A lot of clients come to me specifically because their edges didn't survive their last set of traditional braids.

Install time is the trade-off. A full head of medium knotless braids is a four-to-six-hour appointment, and larger or more elaborate variations can push eight. They typically last six to eight weeks if you stay on top of aftercare. At Studio Salon, knotless is one of the most-requested services I book, and I'll always ask about your scalp history before we start so I can adjust parting size and tension accordingly.

## Feed-In Braids and Tribal Styles

Feed-in braids are cornrows where extensions are added into the braid in small sections as it moves across the scalp, creating a braid that starts thin at the hairline and gradually thickens. The result is a razor-clean look with no visible knot and a natural-looking taper at the front.

Tribal feed-ins build on that technique with more intricate parting — curved paths, designs, beadwork, stacked braids — and are where the style moves from everyday to statement.

Tension is the big thing to watch. Because feed-ins sit close to the scalp, a heavy-handed stylist can cause real edge damage fast. Done right, they should feel firm but never sharp, and there should be no bumps, bleeding, or tenderness within the first day. Feed-ins last two to six weeks depending on how intricate the style is and how well you wrap at night.

Pricing at Studio Salon starts around $80 for a straightforward set of cornrows and runs up to $325 for intricate tribal feed-ins with designs and stacked sections. The upper end reflects real parting and styling time, not just the number of braids.

## Crochet Braids and What They're Good For

Crochet is the technique where we cornrow your natural hair underneath, then use a latch hook to attach loops of pre-made hair — curls, braids, locs, afro textures, whatever look you're going for — directly onto the cornrow base. The install itself is fast, usually two to three hours for a full head once the braid-down is done.

The finished look can range from passing-for-natural curls to dramatic waist-length braids, depending on what hair we use. Crochet is genuinely versatile, and it's often the best protective option for someone who wants the look of long, full braids without committing to eight hours in the chair.

It's also a strong choice if your natural hair is transitioning from relaxed to natural. The cornrow base protects fragile hair while the crochet hair takes the daily styling stress. Lifespan is usually four to six weeks. The one thing to watch for is scalp buildup. Because the cornrows sit underneath the crochet hair, rinsing thoroughly is important at every wash, and a pre-poo rinse before shampoo helps.

## Tension, Install Time, and Lifespan Compared

Those are the three numbers that matter most when you're deciding between styles.

### Quick comparison

1. Knotless braids. Lowest tension. Install four to eight hours. Lifespan six to eight weeks. Best for fragile edges, tender scalps, anyone prioritizing long-term scalp health.
2. Feed-in and tribal feed-ins. Medium tension, higher if done poorly. Install two to five hours. Lifespan two to six weeks. Best for a clean, sharp front, special occasions, and short-term protective periods.
3. Crochet. Lowest scalp-level tension once installed. Install two to three hours plus braid-down. Lifespan four to six weeks. Best for volume without the long time commitment, transitioning hair, and dramatic style changes.

What those numbers don't capture is the feel. Knotless is the most forgiving on tender scalps. Feed-ins give the most polished daytime look. Crochet gives you the biggest range of style options for the install time. Most of my clients rotate between two of the three across a year: a knotless set for summer, crochet for a quick refresh, then feed-ins for a wedding or event. Rotating like that also gives your edges real recovery time between installs.

## Aftercare That Actually Keeps the Style

No matter which of the three you get, the same aftercare basics apply. Sleep on satin, whether that's a bonnet, scarf, or pillowcase, not cotton. Mist your scalp and braids every few days with a light leave-in so the synthetic hair doesn't dry your own hair out. Wash at least every two to three weeks with a diluted shampoo squeezed into the scalp and rinsed thoroughly; braids hold buildup surprisingly fast. Oil your scalp — your scalp, not the length of the hair — with something light like jojoba, tea tree, or a dedicated scalp serum.

Here's the rule I repeat most: take the style out when it's tired, not a week later. Leaving braids in past their window is the single biggest cause of matting and breakage at take-down. If you're not sure how much time you have left on a style, text me a photo and I'll tell you straight. Good aftercare is the difference between taking braids out with healthy hair underneath, or taking them out and starting over.

## Book a Protective Style at Studio Salon

At Studio Salon in Berkeley, I do knotless braids, feed-in and tribal cornrows, and crochet installs for clients across the East Bay. Pricing starts around $80 for a clean set of cornrows and runs up to $325 for intricate tribal feed-ins with designs. Knotless and crochet pricing falls in between and depends on length, size, and the hair you bring.

I always recommend a quick consultation before your first protective install so we can match the style to your hair type, your scalp history, and how long you realistically want to wear it. Call or text (510) 690-5274 to book, or stop by 2902 Sacramento St and let's talk about what would actually work for you.

content:
Retwist frequency is one of the first questions I get in my chair at Studio Salon. Someone sits down, pulls out their phone, and shows me screenshots of advice from three different loc accounts saying three different things. Two weeks. Four weeks. Eight weeks. Only when it gets messy. I've been a loctician in Berkeley long enough to know the honest answer sits somewhere in the middle, and it depends almost entirely on your hair, your lifestyle, and the condition of your roots.

## The 4-to-8 Week Rule (And Why It Isn't One Size Fits All)

The standard answer I give is four to eight weeks, and for most people, that's right. If you have fine, loose-curl hair and your new growth comes in fast, you might sit closer to the four-week mark. If you have dense, tightly coiled hair that locs down easily without much slippage, six to eight weeks is usually your sweet spot. What I push back on hard is the idea that you should be in my chair every two weeks. That's a schedule sold by stylists who want a full book, not one that protects your hair.

It also runs counter to what a retwist is actually for: giving new growth a chance to settle into the existing loc pattern without constant manipulation. Too frequent, and you never let the hair bond. Too infrequent, and the base of the loc starts to blend into a loose, fuzzy halo that's hard to tidy cleanly. Four to eight weeks gives us both — real growth to work with, and a tight, clean result at the scalp.

## What Over-Retwisting Actually Does to Your Roots

Retwisting is mechanical stress on the weakest part of your loc, the new growth at the scalp. Every time we twist, we put tension on hair that's often only a few millimeters long and just starting to pattern. Do that every two weeks, and two things happen.

First, the root gets thin. You'll see the base of the loc taper down to a pencil point, and eventually that loc breaks off at the scalp. I've re-attached more broken locs than I can count, and almost always on clients who came from salons with a two-week retwist habit. Second, the scalp itself gets irritated. Chronic tension pulls on follicles, and over time that shows up as traction alopecia around the hairline and part lines, especially at the edges, where the hair is finest. Once that damage is there, it's slow and frustrating to reverse.

Spacing retwists out isn't laziness. It's the single biggest thing you can do to keep your locs long, thick, and attached to your head.

## Signs Your Locs Are Asking for a Professional Touch-Up

Some people track it by the calendar. I prefer to read the hair. A few cues I look for: your new growth has a visible pattern break where the loose hair meets the mature loc, meaning the two textures aren't blending anymore. Your parts have drifted, and the grid you started with is starting to merge — two locs are marrying at the base, or one is splitting into a Y. You're seeing a halo of frizz an inch or more off the scalp that doesn't lay down even with product and a satin bonnet. Your locs feel loose at the root when you tug gently.

Any of those are signals to book. On the other hand, a little surface fuzz between retwists is normal and actually good. It means your locs are breathing and not being over-manipulated. If you live in Berkeley or anywhere in the East Bay with fog, humidity, and salt air off the Bay, you'll get a bit more frizz than someone in a drier climate, and that's fine. The goal is healthy locs, not plastic-perfect ones.

## Water-Only, Gel, or Butter Retwists

Not every retwist needs product. A water-only retwist is exactly what it sounds like — we mist the roots, twist, and let the hair's own texture do the work. It's my go-to for clients with tightly coiled hair that grips itself, and it leaves zero residue. The trade-off: it doesn't hold as long, maybe two to three weeks of pristine look before the roots start to puff.

Gel retwists use a loc-specific gel, not eco-style, which flakes and builds up, and give you a crisper, longer-lasting hold — three to five weeks before serious fuzz. The trade-off there is buildup if we overdo it, so I use a light hand and always follow with a clarifying wash next visit.

Butter retwists use a shea or mango butter instead of gel. They give shine and moisture, with less hold than gel, and are a great fit for dry scalps and colder months. At Studio Salon I ask every client which finish they want and why, because the right product depends on your hair, not on what's trending on loc-tok this month.

## Interlocking vs. Palm-Rolling: Which Is Right for You?

Palm-rolling is the technique most people picture. We separate the new growth, apply product if we're using any, and roll the root between our palms to train it into the loc below. It's gentle, it gives locs a classic rope-like shape, and it's the method I prefer for mature locs that have a clear pattern.

Interlocking is different. We use a tool, or our fingers, to pass the loc through its own base in a set rotation, literally knitting the new growth into the existing loc. Interlocking lasts much longer between retwists because the root is mechanically locked, not just rolled. That makes it popular with swimmers, athletes, and anyone who washes frequently.

The trade-off: done too often or too tightly, interlocking can weaken the root and create thin spots. I interlock for specific clients — people whose palm-rolled retwists never hold, or those who want six-plus weeks of clean roots. Neither method is better; they're tools. A good loctician picks the right one for your hair, your schedule, and your goals, and isn't afraid to switch between them over the life of your locs.

## Home Care That Extends the Time Between Salon Visits

You can stretch a clean retwist noticeably with a few habits.

### Five home-care moves that actually work

1. Sleep in a satin bonnet or on a satin pillowcase every night, no exceptions. Cotton shreds frizz into your new growth faster than almost anything else.
2. Wash every two to four weeks with a residue-free shampoo, and don't skip it. Clean locs hold their shape better than dirty ones.
3. Mist the roots with water and a light oil like jojoba or grapeseed every few days to keep them supple. Dry hair frizzes; moisturized hair lays down.
4. Re-palm-roll individual locs between salon visits if a few are misbehaving — just those, not the whole head.
5. Avoid heavy creams, butters marketed for loose natural hair, and anything with wax. They build up and cut retwist life in half.

Do those consistently, and you'll comfortably push to six or eight weeks between appointments, with locs that still look fresh when you walk in.

## Book a Retwist at Studio Salon in Berkeley

If you're in Berkeley or anywhere in the East Bay and your locs are asking for attention, I'd love to see you. At Studio Salon, 2902 Sacramento St, I do retwists with palm-rolling or interlocking depending on what your hair actually needs, and I'll always give you an honest timeline for your next visit rather than booking you back in two weeks just because.

First-time clients get a short consultation before we start so I can look at your loc pattern, your scalp, and your goals. Call or text me at (510) 690-5274 to book. Whether you've been locked for six months or sixteen years, I'll meet your hair where it is.
